How we work

A Development Process You Can Follow

Ten stages, each producing something you can read, review or run. You should never have to ask what is happening or what comes next.

Get a Free ConsultationRequest a Quote

01 — Discover

Understand the business goals, current systems, constraints and what success needs to look like.

02 — Plan

Define architecture, technology choices, scope, sequencing and an implementation strategy you can sign off.

03 — Design

Design interfaces and workflows around the people who will use them daily, not around a layout trend.

04 — Develop

Build in reviewable increments with secure, maintainable code and a working demo at the end of each stage.

The full lifecycle

From First Conversation to Ongoing Support

Every stage lists what it produces. If a stage has not produced its outputs, it is not finished — and we do not quietly move on from it.

  1. 01

    Requirement Discovery

    Structured sessions with the people who own the process and the people who run it. We document the exceptions as carefully as the standard path, because that is where projects overrun.

    • Requirement document
    • Scope boundaries
    • Assumptions and open questions
  2. 02

    Business Analysis

    Mapping the current workflow against the proposed one, quantifying the manual effort being removed and identifying which requirements are genuinely essential for the first release.

    • Process maps
    • Prioritised requirements
    • Phase one definition
  3. 03

    Solution Architecture

    Data model, service boundaries, integration points, hosting topology, security model and non-functional requirements agreed in writing before development begins.

    • Architecture diagram
    • Data model
    • Integration map
    • Technology decision record
  4. 04

    UI / UX Design

    Wireframes for the primary journeys, then interface design applied to a component system so every screen is consistent and the build is predictable.

    • Wireframes
    • Interface designs
    • Component library
    • Responsive behaviour spec
  5. 05

    Development

    Delivery in increments, each ending in something demonstrable. Code review on every change, version control discipline, and coding standards agreed at the start rather than argued about later.

    • Working increments
    • Source repository access
    • Code review history
  6. 06

    API & System Integration

    Connecting the build to CRM, ERP, payment providers, internal databases and third-party services, with authentication, retries, idempotency and monitoring designed in.

    • API documentation
    • Integration tests
    • Credential and secret handling plan
  7. 07

    Testing & Quality Assurance

    Functional testing against the requirements, cross-browser and real-device checks, performance testing at realistic data volumes, accessibility review and security checks on inputs and access control.

    • Test results
    • Defect log
    • Performance baseline
    • Accessibility review
  8. 08

    Deployment

    Release through an automated pipeline into a staging environment first, then production, with a written cutover plan, data migration steps and a rehearsed rollback.

    • CI/CD pipeline
    • Cutover plan
    • Rollback procedure
    • Environment documentation
  9. 09

    Monitoring & Measurement

    Application and infrastructure metrics, log aggregation, uptime checks and alerting configured so problems are detected by the monitoring rather than reported by users.

    • Dashboards
    • Alert rules
    • Log retention policy
  10. 10

    Maintenance & Improvement

    Security patching, dependency upgrades, cost reviews, defect resolution and a prioritised backlog for the next round of changes, under an agreed support arrangement.

    • Support agreement
    • Change backlog
    • Periodic review

What we need from you

Projects run late for client-side reasons as often as supplier-side ones. The three that matter most:

  • A decision-maker who can sign off scope
  • Access to the people who run the current process
  • Timely feedback at each review point
  • Credentials and access to existing systems

We will tell you at the start roughly how much of your team's time each stage requires, so it can be planned rather than absorbed.

Discuss your project

Communication

How You Will Know What Is Happening

Process is only useful if you can see it. Four things we commit to on every engagement.

A named contact

One person accountable for the engagement, who knows the technical detail rather than relaying it.

Visible progress

Work tracked in a shared board you can open at any time, not summarised in a monthly email.

Regular demonstrations

Working software at the end of each increment, on a real environment you can click through.

Early warning

If something is going to slip, you hear it when we know — not at the deadline.

Engagement models

How the Work Is Structured

The process is the same either way. What changes is how scope and billing are handled.

Fixed scope, fixed price

Best when requirements are well understood and stable. We define the scope in writing, quote against it, and handle changes through a documented change process.

Dedicated team

A team allocated to your roadmap on a monthly basis, working through a shared backlog. Suits ongoing product development where priorities shift between sprints.

Support & maintenance retainer

An agreed monthly allocation covering monitoring, patching, dependency upgrades, defect fixes and small enhancements, with response expectations set in advance.

Handled as standard

  • Version control and code review on every change
  • Secrets in a managed vault, never in source
  • Automated build and release pipelines
  • Staging environment before production
  • A rehearsed rollback path
  • Monitoring and alerting from day one

Change

What Happens When Requirements Change

They will. Treating that as a failure of planning is what makes it expensive.

Changes are documented, estimated and agreed before the work starts. You see the cost and the schedule impact in writing, then decide whether it is worth it — including the option to defer it to a later phase.

What we avoid is the pattern where small changes are absorbed silently until the timeline has moved by a month and nobody can point to when it happened.
